preamble: Deaspiration of the aspirated alveolar stop [tʰ] to plain [t]. In Ancient Greek it is conditioned by Grassmann's law: when two aspirates occur in successive syllables, the first loses its aspiration, so inherited *tʰ became t before a following aspirate (τίθημι, τριχός, τάφος, ταχύς). In Sylheti it is unconditioned: the loss of the aspiration contrast across the whole stop series turned /tʰ/ into /t/ in every position, as in tʰala > tala 'plate'.

examples.note: Grassmann's law: the reduplicating syllable loses aspiration before the aspirated root.
The root keeps its initial aspirate in the nominative θρίξ thríx, where the final aspirate is lost before s.
Compare θάπτειν tháptein 'to bury', where the second aspirate is lost before the t-suffix.
Compare the comparative θάσσων thássōn 'faster', which keeps the initial aspirate.
Unconditioned deaspiration of the whole stop series, attributed to obstruent weakening; it is linked to the rise of lexical tone.
Word-medial /tʰ/ deaspirates in the same way.
